q: A project to develop a new medical device is starting. What should come first for compliance?
options: Wait until the regulator inspects the finished device and sends findings
Confirm the requirements with legal and compliance experts
Let each developer decide which rules apply to their part
Add compliance work after the first release is out
explanation: Confirming compliance requirements is the first enabler. Governance roles such as legal and compliance officers give insight into regulations, auditing obligations and required processes; involve them early.
ref: The PMI Guide to Business Analysis, 3.3.3.1

links.label: The PMI Guide to Business Analysis, 3.3.3.1

q: Which of these is an external enterprise environmental factor that brings compliance requirements to a project?
options: The company's change control procedure
The project's risk register template
The PMO's lessons learned repository
Local data protection laws
explanation: External EEFs include legal restrictions such as laws on security and data protection, government or industry standards, and public health and safety regulations. The others are organizational process assets.

q: Both the company's own procurement rules and a national safety regulation apply to the project. How do they differ?
options: The law is external; the rules change via policy
Both can be changed by the sponsor at any time
Neither applies if the contract says otherwise
The internal rules always override the regulation in full
explanation: Regulations are external enterprise environmental factors the organization cannot change. Internal policies and procedures are organizational process assets, updated only by following organizational policy.

q: Why does the project manager classify the project's compliance requirements into categories?
options: To reduce the number of requirements the team must meet
To let the team skip the minor categories of rules completely
To see who owns each, how it is checked and its severity
Because the regulator always requires a fixed list
explanation: Classifying compliance categories (security, health and safety, sustainability, regulatory, standards, policy, contractual) shows ownership, the way each is checked, and how serious a breach would be.

q: A team will store patients' health records in a new app. Which compliance category is most directly involved?
options: Contractual service levels
Security and data privacy
Organizational templates
Workmanship standards
explanation: Sensitive personal data falls under laws on security and data protection; it must be secured and collected under a privacy policy.

q: Midway through, the environmental standards for the project's product change, updating its compliance requirements. How should this be treated?
options: As a change to the project's stakeholder register
As a quality defect in a deliverable
As a lesson learned from a past project
As a threat to compliance, managed as a risk
explanation: In the risk practice guide's wind turbine case, changed environmental standards updated the compliance requirements; the risk of noncompliance was treated and then revisited.

q: To save two days, a supervisor proposes skipping the required pressure test on a pipeline section. What should the project manager do?
options: Keep the test and look for time elsewhere
Skip it, since the welds looked fine on inspection
Skip it now and test the section next year instead
Ask the team to vote on whether to skip it
explanation: Required safety tests are compliance obligations. The Code requires acting in the best interests of public health and safety and upholding the rules that govern the work; schedule pressure is a threat to compliance, not a reason to skip.

q: No one on the team understands the new export regulations that apply to the product. What does the risk practice guide suggest?
options: Proceed and learn the rules later from any audit findings
Remove the product from the project's scope at once
Involve experts with regulatory compliance knowledge
Ask the sponsor to accept all compliance risks
explanation: Risk analysis teams should include regulatory compliance competence; external experts or consultants with specialized regulatory knowledge can be advantageous.

q: An agile team works in a regulated industry. How can it build compliance into its everyday work?
options: Leave compliance to one final audit after all releases
Include required compliance in the definition of done
Ignore regulation, since agile values working software
Stop using iterations until all rules are documented
explanation: Where additional documentation or conformance checks are needed, documentation or rigorous test results can be part of what the team delivers; the DoD may include required regulatory compliance being complete.

q: Compliance reviews at large gates keep delaying an agile program. What does the Agile Practice Guide suggest?
options: Add more gates so that each review is smaller and slower
Remove compliance reviews from the program entirely
Hold one big review at the very end of the program
Involve compliance roles early, in small check-ins
explanation: For governance overload: bring audit, security and compliance roles into backlog reviews early, replace large-gate reviews with small, frequent check-ins on completed increments, and automate evidence capture.

q: Which tool determines whether project activities comply with organizational and project policies, processes and procedures?
options: An audit
A burndown chart
A product roadmap
A make-or-buy analysis
explanation: An audit is a structured, independent process used to determine whether project activities comply with organizational and project policies, processes and procedures.

q: The team uses an AI tool to summarize customer complaints that contain personal data. What should the project manager make sure of?
options: The AI's output is used without any human review
The data is shared widely so the tool gives better results
Data is secured and handled under a privacy policy
Customers are not told how their data is used
explanation: AI uses data sets that can be sensitive and regulated by privacy laws, so the data must be secured and collected with a privacy policy in place; use should be transparent and a human accountable.

q: Which compliance-related reason does the Standard list among the conditions under which a project may end?
options: A team member's planned vacation
Legal, regulatory or compliance issues
A change in the meeting schedule
A new version of the project template
explanation: A project usually ends when objectives are met or cannot be met, resources run out, the need disappears, or it is terminated for other reasons such as legal, regulatory or compliance issues.

q: A product fails a safety regulation after launch and must be recalled. In cost of quality terms, what is the recall?
options: A prevention cost
An appraisal cost
A cost of conformance to the rules
An external failure cost
explanation: Failures found after the product reaches the customer are external failure costs: liabilities, warranty work, returns, lost business. They are part of the cost of nonconformance.
ref: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Cost of quality (CoQ)

links.label: PMBOK 8, Guide section 5, Cost of quality (CoQ)

q: Two compliance requirements compete for limited effort. A breach of one would stop the product's sale; a breach of the other would need a minor form. How should effort be allocated?
options: More effort where a breach would be most severe
Equal effort, since all rules have equal weight
Most effort on the requirement easiest to meet
No effort until an auditor raises a finding
explanation: Analyzing the consequences of noncompliance, like a risk, shows where effort matters most. Both requirements must still be met.

q: The business case for a new building says nothing about sustainability. What should the project manager do?
options: Ignore it, since it is not in the formal documents
Add sustainability goals without asking anyone
Raise them, and seek the sponsor's confirmation
Leave them to the operations team after handover
explanation: Sustainability goals should be included in formal documents such as the business case and confirmed by the sponsor. If they are not, the project manager should still encourage discussion of their impact.

q: Where should compliance activities, such as assessing the CO2 emissions of project work, appear in the plan?
options: Only in the final report after closure
In the WBS or the backlog
In the team charter's ground rules
Nowhere, as they belong to operations
explanation: Table 2-6: the WBS or backlog should include activities to manage sustainability, such as assessing and managing CO2 emissions or the impact on local biodiversity.

q: A project would remove trees on its site. Following the sustainability pyramid, which response is the most desirable?
options: Pay a fee to a fund that offsets the loss
Replant the area afterwards
Remove fewer trees than planned
Redesign to avoid removing trees
explanation: The pyramid, from most to least desirable: avoid negative outcomes altogether, minimize them, restore their impacts, compensate or offset them.

q: When does the Standard say compliance can be monitored on a project?
options: During planning, execution and closure
Only at the final acceptance meeting
Only when the regulator visits the site
Only during the first phase
explanation: Sustainability-related KPIs may be included in the charter, business case or contracts, and compliance can be monitored during project planning, execution and closure.

q: Which of these is a measurable way to check how far the project complies?
options: The sponsor's personal impression
The number of meetings held
Open audit findings and compliance KPIs
The length of the requirements document
explanation: Measurable criteria such as KPIs, quality metrics and audit findings on nonconformities show the extent of compliance.

q: Before the project closes, which obligations must it verify as met?
options: Only those that the customer has complained about so far
Contractual, regulatory, legal, social and environmental
Only the internal reporting templates
Only the obligations in the team charter
explanation: Closure verifies that all contractual, regulatory, legal, social and environmental obligations have been met.

q: A subcontractor's work must meet the same safety rules as the project's own work. How can the project make sure of this?
options: Trust the subcontractor's own word on all safety
Put the rules in the contract and inspect the work
Exclude safety from the subcontractor's scope
Check only after an accident has happened
explanation: The rules belong in the procurement agreement; inspections are structured reviews of the contractor's work, and audit rights are written into the contract.

q: How should the project treat the new labeling regulation?
options: Ignore it, as it takes effect only after work starts
Add it to the requirements and manage it as a risk
Ask the contractor to decide whether it applies
Delay the line until the rule changes again
explanation: A new regulation is a compliance requirement and a threat to compliance: add it to the requirements, assess it, and manage it in the risk register.

q: What should happen to the contractor's proposal to skip the hygiene inspection of one machine?
options: Accept it to meet the trade-fair date
Accept it if the contractor signs a written waiver first
Reject it; the inspection is a legal requirement
Let the sales team decide because of the trade fair
explanation: Food safety rules are external compliance requirements that a waiver cannot remove. Noncompliance could stop the line and harm public health; the date must be protected another way.

q: How can the project best measure its water-use commitment?
options: A KPI for water use per unit, checked through the project
The sponsor's impression at the handover meeting
Counting the meetings held about water
A single reading after the line has been running for a year
explanation: Sustainability-related KPIs can be written into the charter, business case or contracts, and compliance monitored during planning, execution and closure.

q: Which TWO are external sources of compliance requirements?
options: Government regulations
Industry standards
The PMO's templates
The project's change control procedure
The team charter
explanation: Government or industry standards and regulations are external enterprise environmental factors. Templates and procedures are internal organizational process assets; the team charter is the team's own agreement.

q: Which THREE are threats to compliance?
options: Rules that change in the middle of the project
No regulatory expertise on the team
Skipping tests under schedule pressure
A definition of done that includes compliance
Auditors involved early in backlog reviews
Evidence captured automatically
explanation: Changing standards, missing compliance competence and shortcuts under pressure threaten compliance. The other three are methods that support it.

q: Which TWO practices does the Agile Practice Guide suggest for compliance in agile work?
options: Bring compliance roles into backlog reviews early
Automate evidence capture where practical
Hold only one large review at the very end
Keep compliance out of the definition of done
Remove all documentation from the work
explanation: Bring audit, security and compliance roles in early, use small frequent check-ins and concise checklists, and automate evidence capture; the DoD may include compliance.

q: Match each compliance category with an example.
explanation: Other categories are regulatory and legal requirements, industry and quality standards, and organizational policies.

q: Complete each statement about compliance.

explanation: Avoid comes first in the pyramid; laws are external enterprise environmental factors; compliance is monitored throughout.
